title: Italian meals, pasta and one-pot dishes
summary: Every meal had pasta, and many dishes were whole meals a working man could carry.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Yeah, pretty much. Pretty much. Pretty much. It was generally that real meat dishes were sundae, roasts, chickens, and that kind of stuff, and always pasta. Right. You know, every meal had pasta. Always pasta. Yeah. Every meal had some kind of pasta. Oh. The main meal, the main dish of the meal. It was either a first dish or a side dish or whatever, depending on how it was fixed. And there were a billion ways to fix pasta.
But your mother knew how to do it.
But in those days you had to.

Yeah, right. Yeah, well, pasta was a staple. It was very inexpensive, good food. Yeah. In fact, most people don't appreciate it now. But a lot of dishes in those days were prepared because it was an entire meal in a dish. Stews, you know. All in one.

All in one. Red beans and rice. Mm-hmm. Macaroni and meatballs. Mm-hmm. And variations on that. For instance, most of the fancier pasta dishes were really done in those days because a working guy could take it from home and have it for lunch. Mm-hmm. And it was everything in one thing, yeah. In fact, chicken cacciatore means hunter's chicken. Mm-hmm. Someone who's a cacciatore is going to go out and catch his things, right? It's a good cognate, in fact. Mm-hmm. Anyway, because it was a meal of the chicken and all the vegetables and all that the guy could take when he went out hunting. Mm-hmm. Again, one little pot and he had everything, that and bread, of course. And wine or beer, depending on whether you were Italian or Irish or Dutch or, you know. Everybody drank in that sense, I think. Just about everybody. But it was part of your meal. It wasn't, you weren't drinking in the sense of drinking. It was part of your meal.
